perspective:
From John Atcitty’s available perspective:

- I am a Heavy Equipment Operator and Alaska Native with a middle-school education. I teach equipment operation at a community center.
- Beverly Yan is my colleague there; she teaches adult education and has a doctorate. We respect each other and often collaborate on projects combining practical and theoretical knowledge.
- In our joint class project, I set up the equipment and told Beverly I hoped it met her expectations. I felt insecure about my education compared with her doctorate. Beverly told me she admired how I handle machines and that education isn’t just degrees—it’s what you do with what you know.
- After Beverly praised my machinery expertise, I felt more confident. I thanked her and suggested a new collaboration: a workshop combining theory and practice. Beverly said she loved the idea, called my practical skills invaluable, and said we could create something special together.
- After a successful collaboration, I worried I might not always meet the high standards we’d set and felt pressured. I told Beverly this. She appreciated my honesty, suggested realistic goals, and said our combined efforts—not perfection—make projects successful.
- After a frank discussion about expectations, I said I was glad we talked and that I could be open with her. Beverly said she respected my openness, trusted my judgment completely, and wanted continued transparency. I believed she valued my honesty and saw me as a reliable partner, which increased my sense of worth.
- Encouraged by our successful collaborations and mutual respect, I felt ambitious. I proposed a larger community-wide event to showcase what we’d achieved together. Beverly called it a fantastic idea, said it was a perfect way to demonstrate our impact, and agreed to start planning.
